PLACEHOLDER: ArchiMate view of SAF actors, roles and collaborations








The SAF distinguishes nine actor types. They are grouped by their position relative to the NSI.









ID
Actor
Position
Description




ACT-01
National Statistical Institute
Internal
The NSI is the organisation that produces official statistics under a legal mandate. It is the central actor in the SAF. The NSI owns the statistical processes and is accountable for the quality and confidentiality of its output. It enters into agreements with data providers, users and partners. In the architecture, the NSI as a whole is the actor that offers business services to society.


ACT-02
Organisational unit
Internal
An organisational unit is a department, division or team within the NSI. Units are the actors that actually carry out the work. Each unit fills one or more roles, such as data collection, methodology or dissemination. The SAF does not prescribe an organisation structure. An NSI maps its own units onto the SAF roles, so that it can see which unit is responsible for which part of the chain.


ACT-03
Data provider
External, supplies data
A data provider is an organisation that supplies data it holds to the NSI. Examples are government agencies with administrative registers, businesses with transaction data, and platform operators. The data is collected for another purpose and reused for statistics. Delivery usually takes place under a legal obligation or a data provision agreement. The NSI cannot control the quality at the source, but it can influence it through agreements and feedback.


ACT-04
Respondent
External, supplies data
A respondent is a person, household or business that provides data directly to the NSI, usually through a survey. Respondents answer questionnaires on the web, by telephone, face to face or on paper. Their burden is a constant concern for the NSI. Respondents are protected by statistical confidentiality: the NSI may not disclose their individual data. The NSI also has a duty to explain why it needs the data and how it uses it.


ACT-05
Data user
External, uses output
A data user is a person or organisation that uses the output of the NSI. Users include policy makers, researchers, journalists, businesses and members of the public. Their needs differ widely. A minister needs a clear figure, a researcher needs microdata under strict conditions, and a developer needs a reliable API. The NSI groups users into segments, so that it can design services and channels for each segment.


ACT-06
Other producer of official statistics
Statistical system
Many countries have more than one producer of official statistics. Examples are central banks, ministries with statistical units and regional statistical offices. The NSI often coordinates this national statistical system. Producers exchange data, align methods and share infrastructure. In the architecture, they are partners in collaborations and sometimes providers or users of each other’s data.


ACT-07
International statistical organisation
Statistical system
International statistical organisations set standards, coordinate statistics across countries and collect national data. Examples are UNECE, Eurostat, the OECD, the IMF and the UN Statistics Division. They require NSIs to deliver data in agreed formats and on agreed dates. They also develop the shared models that the SAF builds on, such as GSBPM and GSIM. For the NSI, they are users, standard setters and partners in collaboration.


ACT-08
Supervisory and legal authority
External, oversees
A supervisory or legal authority oversees whether the NSI acts within the law. Examples are the data protection authority, a national statistics council, the national audit office and the courts. Some authorities grant the legal basis for data collection. Others assess compliance after the fact. The NSI must be able to show these authorities how it handles data, which is one reason why traceability is a core concern of the SAF.


ACT-09
Supplier and service provider
External, supports
A supplier delivers goods or services that the NSI needs but does not produce itself. Examples are software vendors, cloud and hosting providers, field work agencies and trusted third parties for pseudonymisation. Suppliers work under contracts that set requirements for security, confidentiality and continuity. When a supplier processes statistical data, the NSI remains accountable for it. The choice of suppliers is guided by SAF-P01 and by the NSI’s sourcing strategy.






The SAF reference set contains 24 roles in seven groups. The column Process type shows in which of the four process types of a business domain (design, implementation, execution, management) the role mainly works.











ID
Role
Process type
Description




ROL-01
Process owner
Management
The process owner is accountable for the end-to-end performance of a business domain or value stream. This role sets the objectives of the process and decides on changes to it. The process owner makes sure the process has the people, methods and systems it needs. The role receives the quality reports of the management process and acts on them. In the steady-state model, each business domain has one process owner.


ROL-02
Data owner
Management
The data owner is accountable for a dataset or a steady state. This role decides who may access the data, for which purpose and under which conditions. The data owner also approves the retention period and the classification of the data. The role is usually held by a manager in the domain that produces the data. Data ownership is a business role, not an IT role: the data owner answers for the content, not for the storage.


ROL-03
Data steward
Execution
The data steward takes care of data on behalf of the data owner. This role registers datasets in the catalogue and maintains their metadata. The data steward checks that data meets the quality gate before it is registered. The role also handles questions from users and resolves exceptions. Data stewards are the daily point of contact for anyone who wants to find or use a dataset.


ROL-04
Data custodian
Execution
The data custodian is responsible for the safe storage and technical management of data. This role runs storage, backup and access control according to the decisions of the data owner. The custodian carries out retention and disposal. The role does not decide on the use of the data, but makes sure that decisions are applied correctly. In many NSIs, the custodian role is held by an IT or platform team.


ROL-05
Chief data officer
Management
The chief data officer is accountable for data governance across the whole NSI. This role sets the data policy and the governance framework. It assigns the data owner, steward and custodian roles to people and units. The chief data officer chairs or supports the data governance board. The role is the escalation point for conflicts about data that cross domain boundaries.















ID
Role
Process type
Description




ROL-06
Statistical designer
Design
The statistical designer translates information needs into the design of a statistical product. This role defines the outputs, the variables, the population and the required data. The designer specifies the processes that produce the product, in close cooperation with the methodologist. The role is the link between users and production. In some NSIs this role is called product manager.


ROL-07
Methodologist
Design
The methodologist designs and assesses the statistical methods. This role covers sampling, collection methods, editing and imputation, estimation and quality measurement. The methodologist makes sure methods are sound, documented and reproducible. The role also evaluates new methods before they enter production. Specialisations exist for each step of the chain, such as estimation or editing.


ROL-08
Metadata and data architect
Design
The metadata and data architect designs the structure of data and metadata. This role defines data models, metadata schemas and the minimum metadata set of each steady state. The architect makes sure that data from different sources can be combined and compared. The role works with standards such as GSIM and SDMX. It is the bridge between the business architecture and the data architecture.


ROL-09
Classification steward
Design
The classification steward manages the classifications and code lists that the NSI uses. This role maintains national versions of international classifications, such as NACE or ISCO. The steward manages correspondence tables between versions. The role makes sure that all domains use the same version at the same time. Changes to a classification are announced and documented before they take effect.















ID
Role
Process type
Description




ROL-10
Data engineer
Implementation
The data engineer builds the technical processes that move and transform data. This role develops ingestion pipelines, collection channels and processing workflows. The data engineer implements the designs of the statistical designer and the methodologist. The role also builds the automated checks that support the quality gates. The data engineer works closely with the platform engineer, who provides the environment.


ROL-11
Platform engineer
Implementation
The platform engineer provides and runs the environments in which the processes operate. This role configures platforms, storage, connectors and access controls. The platform engineer keeps environments secure, available and up to date. The role supports all value streams but is anchored in VS-09. In many NSIs, the role is also called system configurator or DevOps engineer.


ROL-12
Test manager
Implementation
The test manager plans and coordinates the testing of new or changed processes. This role covers technical tests, integration tests and field tests. The test manager checks that a process produces the expected result before it goes into production. The role reports test results to the process owner. Testing is required before any change to a process that produces a steady state.















ID
Role
Process type
Description




ROL-13
Data collection manager
Execution
The data collection manager runs data collection campaigns. This role plans the collection period, coordinates field staff and monitors response. The manager follows up on non-response and late deliveries. The role also handles contacts with respondents and data providers during collection. The data collection manager reports on collection progress and quality to the process owner.


ROL-14
Data quality analyst
Execution
The data quality analyst checks data during processing. This role runs validation checks, assesses results against the quality gate and logs exceptions. The analyst investigates errors and outliers and proposes corrections. The role documents quality indicators for each version of a dataset. Data quality analysts are active at every handover point in the chain.


ROL-15
Subject-matter statistician
Execution
The subject-matter statistician has in-depth knowledge of a statistical domain, such as labour market or prices. This role interprets results, checks plausibility and explains developments. The statistician carries out or supervises editing, estimation and analysis in the domain. The role writes or reviews the texts that accompany a release. Subject-matter statisticians are the experts that users and journalists turn to.


ROL-16
Disclosure control specialist
Design, Execution
The disclosure control specialist protects the confidentiality of respondents in the output. This role designs and applies disclosure control methods, such as suppression, rounding and noise. The specialist assesses the disclosure risk of tables, microdata and services. The role works at State #4 and at the gate to State #5. No output is released without a disclosure check that this role has approved.


ROL-17
Release manager
Execution
The release manager controls the publication of statistical output. This role makes sure that releases follow the release calendar and the embargo rules. The release manager checks that the output has been approved and has passed disclosure control. The role coordinates the release across channels, such as the website, the API and press releases. Equal access for all users at the moment of release is a key responsibility.















ID
Role
Process type
Description




ROL-18
Quality manager
Management
The quality manager is responsible for the quality framework of the NSI. This role defines quality indicators and monitors them across the chain. The quality manager produces quality reports and leads improvement actions. The role supports process owners in the management process of their domains. It also prepares the NSI for quality reviews, such as peer reviews against the European Statistics Code of Practice.


ROL-19
Compliance officer
Management
The compliance officer makes sure that the NSI complies with laws and regulations. This role covers statistical law, data protection law and other applicable rules. The officer checks new processes and methods against compliance criteria before they go into production. The role keeps the legal register up to date. In many NSIs the data protection officer is a specific form of this role.


ROL-20
Security officer
Management
The security officer is responsible for information security and continuity. This role defines security measures and monitors their application. The officer manages security incidents and leads recovery when something goes wrong. The role assesses the security of new solutions and suppliers. It works closely with the platform engineer and the compliance officer.


ROL-21
Auditor
Management
The auditor checks independently whether processes and controls work as intended. This role can be internal, such as an internal audit department, or external, such as the national audit office or a certification body. The auditor reviews evidence, such as logs, quality reports and lineage records. The role reports findings to management and to supervisory authorities. Its work depends on the traceability that the SAF builds into the chain.















ID
Role
Process type
Description




ROL-22
Dissemination and service manager
Design, Execution
The dissemination and service manager designs and manages the services through which users receive output. This role covers publications, open data, APIs and microdata access. The manager defines channels and formats for each user segment. The role manages the portfolio of services and their service levels. It works with the release manager on the timing and with the relationship manager on user needs.


ROL-23
Relationship manager
Execution
The relationship manager maintains the relationships with key external actors. These include data providers, major users, partners and international organisations. The manager collects needs, feedback and complaints, and passes them to the right roles. The role negotiates and maintains agreements, such as data provision agreements. Relationship managers make sure that the NSI speaks with one voice to each partner.















ID
Role
Process type
Description




ROL-24
Enterprise architect
Design, Management
The enterprise architect develops and maintains the enterprise architecture of the NSI. This role translates strategy into architecture and uses the SAF as its reference. The architect advises on investments and reviews projects against the architecture principles. The role supports the architecture board and keeps the architecture repository up to date. It is the role that realises the capability Architecture management.

















ID
Collaboration
Members
Type
Description




COL-01
Data provision partnership
NSI, data provider, relationship manager, data owner
External, permanent
A data provision partnership is the long-term cooperation between the NSI and a data provider. It goes beyond a single delivery. The partners agree on content, format, timing and quality of the data. They also agree on how to handle changes at the source, such as a new system or a new definition. A good partnership reduces the burden for the provider and improves the quality for the NSI.


COL-02
National statistical system
NSI, other producers of official statistics
External, permanent
The national statistical system is the cooperation between all producers of official statistics in one country. The NSI usually coordinates it. The members align methods, classifications and release practices, so that national statistics are consistent. They exchange data and sometimes share infrastructure. The cooperation is often based on the national statistics law.


COL-03
International statistical cooperation
NSI, international statistical organisations, other NSIs
External, permanent
International statistical cooperation is the collaboration between NSIs and international organisations. It covers the development of standards, the exchange of data and the joint development of tools. The SAF itself is a product of this cooperation. Members take part in working groups, such as those of UNECE and the European Statistical System. The cooperation helps NSIs avoid building the same solution many times.


COL-04
Research access partnership
NSI, research institutes, data owner, disclosure control specialist
External, permanent
A research access partnership gives researchers access to microdata under strict conditions. The NSI, research institutes and sometimes funding bodies take part. The partners agree on who may access which data, for which purpose and in which environment. Output is checked for disclosure risk before it leaves the secure environment. The partnership supports science while protecting the confidentiality of respondents.


COL-05
Statistical product team
Statistical designer, methodologist, data engineer, subject-matter statistician
Internal, permanent or temporary
A statistical product team brings together the roles needed to design, build and run a statistical product. It typically includes a statistical designer, a methodologist, a data engineer and a subject-matter statistician. The team can be permanent for a product or temporary for a redesign. Working as one team shortens the path from design to production. It also makes sure that methodological and technical choices are made together.


COL-06
Data governance board
Chief data officer, data owners, data stewards, compliance officer
Internal, permanent
The data governance board steers data management across the NSI. The chief data officer chairs it, and data owners, data stewards and the compliance officer take part. The board sets data policies, resolves conflicts between domains and monitors compliance. It decides on access requests that cross domain boundaries. The board makes sure that the steady-state model is applied consistently.


COL-07
Architecture board
Enterprise architect, process owners, CIO or CTO
Internal, permanent
The architecture board steers the enterprise architecture of the NSI. The enterprise architect, process owners and the CIO or CTO take part. The board reviews projects against the architecture principles and the target architecture. It decides on deviations through a documented dispensation process. The board keeps the architecture aligned with the strategy and with the SAF.

title: Business Architecture
text:
A business process is a sequence of activities that produces a defined result for a customer, a stakeholder or another process. A process has a trigger, a start and an end. It has inputs and outputs, and it uses the knowledge and resources of one or more business functions. Processes describe how work flows, step by step. They are the part of the business architecture that people recognise most directly in their daily work.
Processes can be decomposed. A high-level process consists of sub-processes, which can in turn be broken down further. The SAF describes processes at two levels: process phases or process groups, and the sub-processes within them. More detailed levels, such as work instructions, are specific to each NSI and fall outside the SAF.
A process is not the same as a value stream stage. A value stream stage describes the value that is added. A process describes the work that adds it. One stage is usually realised by several processes, and one process can contribute to several stages.



Why the SAF describes business processes
Processes are where architecture meets daily operations. A shared process model lets NSIs compare how they work, reuse each other’s solutions and discuss improvements in the same terms. It also links the strategic layer to the systems: value streams are realised by processes, and processes are supported by application services. Without a process model, it is hard to show which system supports which part of the work, or where a change in method affects other steps.
How business processes fit into an NSI’s own architecture
The core of the SAF process model is GSBPM, which most NSIs already know. The SAF adds three process groups that GSBPM does not describe in detail: data management and lifecycle, microdata services and data spaces. An NSI adopts the process model as a reference, maps its own processes onto it and adds its own lower levels. A national process for, say, the monthly price index can then be traced to the SAF sub-processes it implements. The SAF does not prescribe the order of sub-processes. GSBPM is not a strict sequence: sub-processes can be skipped, repeated or run in parallel.

The statistical production processes follow the eight phases of GSBPM. Each phase is described first, followed by its sub-processes. The descriptions are paraphrased from GSBPM, a model of UNECE published under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence (CC BY 4.0).










ID
Process
Description




PRD-1
Specify Needs
This phase starts when a new statistical need is identified, or when an existing product needs review. It establishes what users need and whether the NSI can meet that need. The phase explores options, including the use of data that already exists. It ends with a decision on whether to proceed, based on a business case. For existing products that run regularly, this phase is usually carried out only when a review is due.


PRD-1.1
Identify needs
This sub-process investigates which statistics are needed and what they are needed for. The trigger can be a new policy question, a legal requirement or a user request. It also looks at changes in the needs for existing statistics. Input comes from users, stakeholders, legislation and earlier evaluations. The result is a first description of the need.


PRD-1.2
Consult and confirm needs
This sub-process consults users and stakeholders to understand the need in detail. It checks what exactly they want to know, at which level of detail and how often. It also explores which constraints apply, such as timing or budget. The NSI and the users confirm the need together. The result is a confirmed and documented set of needs.


PRD-1.3
Establish output objectives
This sub-process translates the confirmed needs into output objectives. It defines which statistics will be produced and which quality they must meet. Legal and confidentiality constraints are taken into account. The objectives are realistic for the data and resources that are available. The result is the basis for the design of the outputs.


PRD-1.4
Identify concepts
This sub-process clarifies the concepts to be measured, from the point of view of the users. A concept such as “household income” or “unemployment” needs a clear meaning. The sub-process checks whether existing statistical concepts can be reused. Concepts may not yet match the definitions that data sources use. That mismatch is resolved later, in the design phase.


PRD-1.5
Check data availability and suitability
This sub-process checks whether existing data sources can meet the need. It looks at internal data, administrative data, data spaces and other external sources. For each source, it assesses quality, coverage, timeliness and legal conditions. Reusing existing data comes before new collection, in line with SAF-P08. The result shows which gaps remain that new data must fill.


PRD-1.6
Prepare and submit business case
This sub-process documents the findings of the phase in a business case. The business case describes the need, the proposed solution, the costs and the benefits. It also lists risks and alternatives. The business case is submitted to management for a decision. Approval starts the design phase.














ID
Process
Description




PRD-2
Design
This phase designs the statistical product and the process that produces it. It covers outputs, variables, collection, sampling, processing, analysis and dissemination. It also defines the metadata and the quality criteria. Designs reuse existing standards, methods and components wherever possible. The results are the specifications for the build phase.


PRD-2.1
Design outputs and dissemination
This sub-process designs the statistical outputs in detail. It defines tables, datasets, indicators and their metadata. It also designs how and through which channels the outputs will be disseminated. Disclosure control requirements are taken into account from the start. The design follows the output objectives from PRD-1.3.


PRD-2.2
Design variables
This sub-process defines the variables to be collected and to be derived. It specifies their definitions, the types of statistical units and the classifications that apply. Existing variables and classifications are reused where possible. Each variable gets metadata that describes its meaning. The result is a variable list that all later phases use.


PRD-2.3
Design collection
This sub-process determines how the data will be collected. It chooses the sources, the collection modes and the instruments, such as questionnaires or data interfaces. For administrative data and data spaces, it designs the agreements and delivery formats. Respondent burden is kept as low as possible. The design also covers the metadata and paradata to be captured.


PRD-2.4
Design frame and sample
This sub-process defines the target population and the frame from which units are selected. It designs the sampling method and the sample size, where a sample is used. For register-based statistics, it defines how the population is derived from the registers. Coverage problems in the frame are identified and addressed. The result is the method used later in PRD-4.1.


PRD-2.5
Design processing and analysis
This sub-process designs the methods for processing and analysis. It covers integration, coding, validation, editing, imputation, derivation, weighting and estimation. It also designs the methods for disclosure control. Methods are documented so that results can be reproduced. The designs are reviewed by methodologists before they are built.


PRD-2.6
Design production systems and workflows
This sub-process designs the end-to-end workflow of the statistical process. It defines which systems and components are needed for each step. It avoids gaps and duplication between steps. Reuse of existing components and shared platforms comes first, in line with SAF-P01. The result is the blueprint for the build phase.














ID
Process
Description




PRD-3
Build
This phase builds and tests the production solution. It assembles the components, configures the workflows and tests the whole process. Components are reused where possible and built only where needed. The phase ends when the process is ready for production. For regular products, this phase is only needed when something changes.


PRD-3.1
Reuse or build collection instruments
This sub-process builds or reuses the instruments for data collection. Examples are electronic questionnaires, data delivery interfaces and connectors to data spaces. It follows the design from PRD-2.3. Instruments are tested for usability and correctness. The result is a set of instruments ready for collection.


PRD-3.2
Reuse or build processing and analysis components
This sub-process builds or reuses the components for processing and analysis. Examples are validation rules, imputation routines and estimation programmes. The components implement the methods designed in PRD-2.5. Shared components that other products already use are preferred. Each component is documented and version-controlled.


PRD-3.3
Reuse or build dissemination components
This sub-process builds or reuses the components for dissemination. Examples are table templates, publication workflows and API endpoints. It follows the design from PRD-2.1. Shared dissemination platforms are used where possible. The components are tested together with the output systems.


PRD-3.4
Configure workflows
This sub-process configures the workflows that connect the components. It sets up the order of steps, the data flows and the transformations. It also configures the registration of data in the steady states. Configuration is preferred over custom code. The result is an executable workflow.


PRD-3.5
Test production systems
This sub-process tests the assembled systems and their interactions. It checks that components work together and handle errors correctly. It also tests performance and security. Test results are documented and reported to the process owner. Defects are fixed before the process goes live.


PRD-3.6
Test statistical business process
This sub-process tests the whole statistical process in practice. It can take the form of a pilot or a field test with real data. It checks that the process produces results of the expected quality. Problems found in the test lead to changes in design or build. The process owner decides whether the process is ready.


PRD-3.7
Finalise production systems
This sub-process puts the process and its systems into production. It completes the documentation and trains the staff involved. It transfers the systems to the teams that will run and maintain them. The metadata of the process is registered. From this moment, the process can run in the collect to disseminate phases.














ID
Process
Description




PRD-4
Collect
This phase collects or acquires the data, metadata and paradata needed for the product. It covers surveys, administrative data, data from data spaces and other sources. Data is received securely and checked for completeness. The phase ends when the data is stored and registered as raw data. In the steady-state model, this phase produces State #1.


PRD-4.1
Create frame and select sample
This sub-process creates the frame for this iteration of the process. It applies the method designed in PRD-2.4 to the current population. Where a sample is used, it draws the sample. The quality of the frame and the sample is checked. The result is the list of units from which data will be collected.


PRD-4.2
Set up collection
This sub-process makes sure that people, processes and systems are ready to collect. It prepares the instruments, trains interviewers and informs respondents or data providers. It checks that agreements and access rights are in place. Collection channels are tested before collection starts. The collection period is planned and communicated.


PRD-4.3
Run collection
This sub-process carries out the collection. Respondents complete questionnaires, and data providers deliver their data. Progress and response are monitored continuously. Non-response is followed up within the agreed strategy. Paradata about the collection is recorded.


PRD-4.4
Finalise collection
This sub-process loads the collected data and metadata into a secure environment. It checks integrity, completeness and structure at intake. It registers the data as a new version of raw data. Delivery problems are reported to the data provider. The collection is closed when all expected data has been received or written off.














ID
Process
Description




PRD-5
Process
This phase turns the collected data into microdata that is ready for analysis. It integrates, classifies, checks, corrects and derives data. It also calculates weights and aggregates. The phase runs across several business domains of the steady-state model. It produces States #2 and #3, and the first aggregates of State #4.


PRD-5.1
Integrate data
This sub-process combines data from one or more sources into a consistent dataset. It links records that describe the same unit, using agreed keys. It resolves overlaps and conflicts between sources. Linkage uses pseudonymised keys where personal data is involved. The result is an integrated dataset with documented linkage quality.


PRD-5.2
Classify and code
This sub-process assigns codes from standard classifications to the data. Examples are codes for economic activity, occupation or region. Coding can be automatic, manual or a mix of both. The classification versions used are recorded in the metadata. Coding quality is checked and documented.


PRD-5.3
Review and validate
This sub-process checks the data for errors, outliers and inconsistencies. It applies the validation rules designed in PRD-2.5. It flags records that need attention. Some checks run automatically, others need expert review. The result is a dataset with quality flags and a list of issues.


PRD-5.4
Edit and impute
This sub-process corrects incorrect values and fills in missing values. Corrections follow editing rules, and missing values are imputed with documented methods. Every change is recorded, so that the original value can always be traced. The impact of editing and imputation on the results is measured. The result is a complete and consistent dataset.


PRD-5.5
Derive new variables and units
This sub-process creates variables and units that were not collected directly. Examples are age groups, household composition or enterprise groups. Derivations follow the specifications from PRD-2.2. Derived variables get their own metadata. The derivation rules are documented and reusable.


PRD-5.6
Calculate weights
This sub-process calculates weights for the records in the dataset. Weights correct for the sample design, non-response and coverage. They follow the method designed in PRD-2.5. The quality of the weights is checked. The weights are stored with the microdata.


PRD-5.7
Calculate aggregates
This sub-process calculates totals and other aggregates from the microdata. It applies the weights and the estimation methods. It can also combine lower-level aggregates into higher levels. Accuracy measures are calculated alongside the estimates. The result is the first version of the statistics.


PRD-5.8
Finalise data files
This sub-process combines the results of the phase into the files used for analysis. It checks that the files are complete and consistent. It registers the processed microdata as a new version in the steady state. The metadata of the files is completed. The files are now ready for the analysis phase.














ID
Process
Description




PRD-6
Analyse
This phase turns the processed data into statistical outputs and checks that they are fit for release. It prepares draft outputs, validates them and explains them. It also applies disclosure control. The phase ends with the approval of the content for release. In the steady-state model, it completes State #4.


PRD-6.1
Prepare draft outputs
This sub-process transforms the data files into draft statistical outputs. Examples are tables, indicators, time series and charts. It also prepares the methodological notes that go with them. Drafts follow the output design from PRD-2.1. They are the input for validation and interpretation.


PRD-6.2
Validate outputs
This sub-process checks the draft outputs for quality and plausibility. It compares results with earlier periods, other sources and expectations. It checks them against the quality framework. Unexpected results are investigated before they are accepted. The result is a set of validated outputs with documented quality.


PRD-6.3
Interpret and explain outputs
This sub-process interprets the outputs and explains what they mean. Subject-matter experts describe developments and their causes. Deeper analyses may be carried out to support the explanation. The interpretation must be neutral and based on the data. The result is the content for publications and press releases.


PRD-6.4
Apply disclosure control
This sub-process makes sure that outputs do not reveal information about individual respondents. It applies the disclosure control methods designed in PRD-2.5. Examples are suppression of cells, rounding and adding noise. The disclosure risk is assessed and documented. No output is released without passing this check.


PRD-6.5
Finalise outputs
This sub-process makes sure that the statistics are fit for use. It completes the outputs and their metadata. It checks that all quality and confidentiality requirements are met. The content is approved for release by the responsible role. The approved outputs are registered as statistics ready for dissemination.














ID
Process
Description




PRD-7
Disseminate
This phase publishes the statistical products and supports users. It updates the output systems, produces the products and releases them. It also promotes the products and answers user questions. Equal access for all users at the moment of release is a core rule. In the steady-state model, this phase produces State #5.


PRD-7.1
Update output systems
This sub-process loads the approved data and metadata into the systems used for dissemination. Examples are databases behind the website, open data portals and APIs. It checks that the data is loaded correctly and remains embargoed until release. Format and structure follow the dissemination design. The result is output that is ready for release.


PRD-7.2
Produce dissemination products
This sub-process produces the products that users receive. Examples are press releases, publications, tables, visualisations and datasets. It follows the design from PRD-2.1. Products are checked for correctness and consistency before release. The result is a set of products ready to publish.


PRD-7.3
Release dissemination products
This sub-process releases the products to users. It follows the release calendar and the embargo rules. All channels are updated at the same moment, so that no user gets an advantage. Errors found after release are corrected openly. The release is logged for accountability.


PRD-7.4
Promote dissemination products
This sub-process brings the products to the attention of users. It uses channels such as social media, newsletters and events. It targets the user segments that have an interest in the product. Promotion helps users find and understand the statistics. Its effect is monitored.


PRD-7.5
Provide user support
This sub-process answers questions and requests from users. Questions are registered and answered within agreed times. Frequent questions lead to better documentation or products. Requests for tailor-made data are handled according to confidentiality rules. Feedback from users is passed on to the product owners.














ID
Process
Description




PRD-8
Evaluate
This phase evaluates a specific run of the statistical process. It collects evidence, assesses quality and performance, and agrees on improvements. Evaluation can take place after every run or at set intervals. Its results feed back into the next run or into a redesign. The phase is part of the management process type of each business domain.


PRD-8.1
Gather evaluation inputs
This sub-process collects the material for the evaluation. Examples are quality indicators, paradata, process logs, user feedback and staff comments. The inputs come from all earlier phases. They are brought together in one place. The result is a complete evidence base for the evaluation.


PRD-8.2
Conduct evaluation
This sub-process analyses the inputs and draws conclusions. It assesses the quality of the outputs and the efficiency of the process. It compares results with targets and with earlier runs. Strengths and weaknesses are identified. The result is an evaluation report or dashboard.


PRD-8.3
Agree an action plan
This sub-process agrees on actions to improve the process. It sets priorities, owners and deadlines. Actions can lead to small changes or to a full redesign. Progress on the actions is monitored. The action plan is the input for the next cycle.







Overarching processes run across all phases of statistical production. They are not steps in the sequence. They apply to every phase, and to every product. They are based on the overarching processes of GSBPM.








ID
Process
Description




OVA-1
Quality Management
This process assesses and controls the quality of products and processes. It applies the quality framework of the NSI in every phase. It defines quality indicators, measures them and reports on them. Quality problems lead to corrective actions. The process supports the NSI-wide quality management function.


OVA-2
Metadata Management
This process creates, updates, uses and archives statistical metadata in all phases. Metadata describes concepts, variables, classifications, methods and processes. It is captured when it is created, not afterwards. Metadata is shared through a catalogue, so that others can find and understand the data. The process applies SAF-P09 No data without metadata and classification.


OVA-3
Data Management
This process manages data throughout its life cycle in production. It covers storage, security, versioning, retention and disposal. It makes sure that data is available to the right people at the right time. The SAF details this process in group C, Data management and lifecycle processes. The process applies the design rules of the steady-state model.


OVA-4
Process Data Management
This process records and uses data about the execution of the statistical process. Examples are paradata from collection, logs of processing steps and timings. Process data shows how the process actually ran. It is used for monitoring, evaluation and audit. It is also the basis for lineage: the trace from output back to source.


OVA-5
Knowledge Management
This process maintains the knowledge needed to run the production process. It keeps documentation, methods and procedures up to date. It makes sure that recurring processes can be repeated in the same way. It also captures lessons learned from evaluations. Knowledge management reduces the dependence on individual staff members.


OVA-6
Data Supplier Management
This process manages the technical and operational relationship with data suppliers during production. It covers delivery schedules, formats, quality feedback and problem resolution. It keeps track of the burden placed on suppliers. It works within the agreements made at corporate level. Good supplier management improves data quality and reduces delays.






These processes manage data as an asset, across products and over its whole life. They detail the overarching process OVA-3 Data Management. They follow the life cycle of a steady state: promotion, gate, registration, use, revision and retirement. They apply to every reference model for the data value chain.








ID
Process
Description




DLM-1
Plan and design data assets
This process decides which data assets the NSI needs and how they are structured. It defines datasets, their owners, their classification and their place in the steady states. It is triggered by a new product, a new source or a change in the data architecture. Planning prevents duplicate datasets and unclear ownership. The result is a documented design for each data asset.


DLM-2
Promote data through a quality gate
This process submits a dataset to the quality gate of a steady state. It checks the dataset against the gate criteria, such as completeness, structure and required metadata. The outcome is acceptance, conditional acceptance with quality flags, or rejection. Rejected data returns to the producing domain or the data provider. The process makes sure that only data of known quality enters a steady state.


DLM-3
Register and catalogue data
This process registers an accepted dataset as a new, immutable version. It assigns a persistent identifier and records the metadata in the catalogue. It publishes an event that tells consuming domains a new version is available. Registration makes the data findable for authorised users. Without registration, data cannot be handed over.


DLM-4
Classify and protect data
This process assigns a security classification to each dataset, for availability, integrity and confidentiality. It applies the protection measures that follow from the classification. It also applies pseudonymisation or other privacy measures where required. Classification is reviewed when data moves to the next steady state. The process applies SAF-P09, SAF-P10 and SAF-P11.


DLM-5
Store and version data
This process stores each registered version of a dataset safely. Earlier versions are kept, not overwritten. Backups and recovery are arranged according to the availability requirements. Storage follows the retention policy of each steady state. The process makes it possible to reproduce any statistic from the data it was built on.


DLM-6
Provide data for reuse
This process gives authorised internal users access to registered data. A user requests access, and the data owner decides on the request. Access is granted for a stated purpose and a set period. Use is logged. The process applies SAF-P08 Data is shared property, within the limits of confidentiality.


DLM-7
Revise data
This process handles corrections and redeliveries of data that is already registered. A correction creates a new version that passes the same quality gate. Consumers of the earlier version are notified. They decide whether to reprocess their own data. The reason for each revision is recorded.


DLM-8
Monitor data quality, lineage and use
This process monitors registered data over time. It tracks quality indicators, the lineage from source to output, and how the data is used. It detects problems, such as declining quality or unauthorised use. It reports to data owners and the data governance board. The results feed into improvements and audits.


DLM-9
Manage reference and master data
This process manages the data that other data depends on. Examples are classifications, code lists, statistical registers and population frames. It controls versions and publishes changes in advance. It makes sure that all domains use the same version at the same time. Errors in reference data affect many products, so changes are tested carefully.


DLM-10
Archive and preserve data
This process transfers data that must be kept long-term to an archive. It selects what must be preserved, based on legal obligations and reproducibility needs. It makes sure that archived data remains readable and understandable, with its metadata. Access to archived data is controlled. The process follows national archives legislation.


DLM-11
Dispose of data
This process deletes data at the end of its retention period. It checks that no statistic or obligation still depends on the data. Deletion covers all copies, including backups and working copies. Keys used for pseudonymisation are destroyed when they are no longer needed. Each disposal is recorded, so that it can be shown in an audit.






Microdata services give researchers controlled access to microdata for statistical and scientific research. Access takes place under strict conditions, usually in a secure processing environment. The NSI remains responsible for confidentiality throughout. These processes realise part of VS-06 Dissemination and Service Delivery and work within the collaboration COL-04 Research access partnership.








ID
Process
Description




MDS-1
Authorise institutions and researchers
This process decides which institutions and researchers may use microdata services. It checks the legal status of the institution and the qualifications of the researchers. Authorised institutions sign an agreement that sets the conditions of use. Researchers confirm that they will respect confidentiality. Authorisations are reviewed periodically and can be withdrawn.


MDS-2
Assess access applications
This process handles an application to use microdata for a specific research project. The applicant describes the purpose, the data needed and the expected outputs. The NSI checks the legal basis, the public interest and whether the data requested is necessary. It also checks for special categories of data that need extra approval. The result is an approval with conditions, or a reasoned refusal.


MDS-3
Prepare research datasets
This process prepares the datasets for an approved project. It selects only the data that the project needs. It replaces identifiers with project-specific pseudonyms, so that data cannot be linked across projects. Where the project brings its own data, the NSI links it under the same rules. The prepared dataset is registered with its metadata and lineage.


MDS-4
Provide a secure processing environment
This process sets up the environment in which researchers work with the data. The environment prevents data from leaving without control. Access is limited to the authorised researchers of the project. Tools and computing power are provided as agreed. All activity in the environment is logged.


MDS-5
Facilitate privacy-preserving analysis
This process supports analysis without moving the data into one place. Examples are federated analysis, where the algorithm goes to the data, and secure multi-party computation. These techniques are used when partners cannot or may not share their data. The NSI defines the trust model, the linkage method and the output rules for each setup. The process extends microdata services to data that the NSI does not hold itself.


MDS-6
Support researchers
This process helps researchers use the data and the environment correctly. It answers questions about content, metadata and methods. It explains the rules for confidentiality and output. It handles technical problems in the environment. Good support reduces errors and speeds up research.


MDS-7
Check and release output
This process checks every output before it leaves the secure environment. It applies disclosure control rules to tables, models and other results. It also checks for risks across outputs, such as differencing between similar results. Outputs that pass are released to the researcher. Outputs that fail are returned with an explanation.


MDS-8
Monitor use and compliance
This process monitors whether institutions and researchers follow the conditions of use. It reviews logs, outputs and incidents. It also tracks the use of query or disclosure budgets where these apply. Breaches lead to measures, up to withdrawal of the authorisation. The results are reported to the data owner and to supervisory authorities where required.


MDS-9
Close projects
This process ends a research project in a controlled way. It removes the project’s data and workspace. It destroys the project-specific pseudonymisation keys. It archives what must be kept for reproducibility, such as the code and the approved outputs. The closure is recorded, so that it can be shown in an audit.






A data space is a shared environment in which organisations exchange data under common rules, while each keeps control over its own data. Examples are the European data spaces for health, mobility or public administration. An NSI can take part as a data provider, as a data user, or both. Some NSIs also act as an access body that grants access to data on behalf of other data holders. That role is not covered by the SAF reference processes. The data space processes realise parts of VS-01 Data Acquisition and Ingestion and VS-06 Dissemination and Service Delivery.








ID
Process
Description




DSP-1
Join a data space
This process prepares the NSI to take part in a data space. It assesses the rules of the data space against the NSI’s legal mandate and policies. It signs the participation agreement and obtains the required identity and trust credentials. It sets up the technical connection, for example through a connector. The NSI decides in advance whether it joins as provider, as user, or as both.


DSP-2
Publish data offerings
This process makes NSI data visible in the data space. It describes datasets in the data space catalogue, using agreed metadata standards. It states the conditions under which the data may be used. Only data that the NSI may share under its legal mandate is offered. The offering is kept up to date when the data or the conditions change.


DSP-3
Agree data use conditions
This process agrees on the terms of a specific data exchange. Provider and user agree on purpose, duration, permitted use and security measures. The terms are recorded in a contract or usage policy that machines can check where possible. The NSI checks that the terms fit its confidentiality rules. Without agreed terms, no data is exchanged.


DSP-4
Exchange data under usage control
This process carries out the agreed data exchange. Data is transferred securely, or analysed where it resides without transfer. Usage control enforces the agreed conditions where the technology allows it. Every exchange is logged. Incoming data enters the NSI through the data acquisition process and is registered as raw data.


DSP-5
Monitor compliance and report
This process monitors whether the NSI’s own exchanges follow the rules of the data space. It checks agreements, logs, incidents and the use of data. It reports security incidents within the legal deadlines. It also checks whether partners respect the conditions agreed for NSI data. Breaches lead to measures, including suspension of the exchange.


DSP-6
Participate in data space governance
This process covers the NSI’s role in steering the data space. The NSI takes part in governance bodies and contributes to the rules and standards. It brings in statistical expertise on metadata, classifications, quality and confidentiality. It also evaluates whether participation still serves its mandate. When the NSI leaves a data space, this process arranges a controlled exit.

title: Business Architecture
text:
A business function is a grouping of behaviour based on the knowledge, skills and resources it needs. A function describes what the organisation does on a continuous basis. It has no start or end, and it does not depend on the order in which work is done. Manage metadata is a function: it exists as long as the NSI exists, whatever process happens to use it. Functions are stable, because the competences an organisation needs change much more slowly than its procedures.
Functions differ from processes. A process is a sequence of activities with a trigger and a result. A function is a lasting area of competence that processes draw on. One process uses several functions, and one function serves several processes. The mapping at the end of this section shows how they relate.
Functions also differ from capabilities. A capability, in the Strategy layer, describes an ability the NSI has or needs. A function, in the business layer, describes the behaviour that delivers that ability. Functions realise capabilities. In practice, the two often have similar names, but they serve different purposes: capabilities support planning and investment, functions support the design of the organisation and its processes.



Why the SAF describes business functions
Functions give a stable picture of the organisation that does not change with every reorganisation or new system. They are the natural basis for assigning responsibilities: each function has an owner who maintains the competence. They also help to compare NSIs. Two NSIs may have very different processes and departments, but they will recognise the same functions. Finally, functions make gaps visible. A function that no one owns is a competence that the organisation risks losing.
How business functions fit into an NSI’s own architecture
An NSI maps its departments and teams onto the SAF functions. The mapping shows which unit carries which function, and where functions are spread over several units. An NSI can also map the SAF functions onto a national function model, such as a government-wide model for business support. Functions that are specific to the NSI’s mandate are added as extensions. The SAF function areas for statistical production, data management, microdata services and data spaces are specific to official statistics. The business support area is generic and can be replaced by a national model where one exists.

FUN-3
Statistical Production
This area produces official statistics, from the first design to the release. It is the core of the NSI’s mandate. The statistical production processes (PRD) realise this area. Its functions follow the main kinds of statistical work: design, collection, processing, estimation, confidentiality and dissemination. Each function brings together the specialist knowledge for that kind of work.
1


FUN-3.1
Design and build statistical products
This function designs statistical products and the processes that produce them. It translates information needs into outputs, variables, methods and workflows. It also builds and tests the production solution. It works closely with methodology and with the users of the product. The function owns the design of each product over its life cycle.
1.1


FUN-3.2
Collect and acquire data
This function obtains the data that statistical products need. It runs surveys, receives administrative data and acquires data from other sources, including data spaces. It makes sure that data arrives complete, on time and under the right agreements. It keeps respondent burden as low as possible. The function delivers data into the first steady state.
1.2


FUN-3.3
Process statistical data
This function turns raw data into reliable microdata. It integrates, standardises, codes, validates, edits and imputes data. It also derives new variables and units. It applies the methods designed for each product. The function produces standardised and processed microdata.

Estimate and analyse

1.3.5, 1.3.6, 1.4


FUN-3.5
Protect statistical confidentiality
This function makes sure that no output reveals information about individual respondents. It sets the confidentiality rules and the methods for disclosure control. It applies them to tables, microdata files and services. It assesses disclosure risks in new types of output. The function works across all products and channels.
1.3.7


FUN-3.6
Disseminate statistics
This function brings statistics to users. It manages the release calendar, the publication channels and the products. It makes sure that all users get access at the same moment. It also supports users in finding and understanding the statistics. The function produces released data.

FUN-7
Data Management
This area manages data and metadata as assets of the NSI. It covers governance, metadata, the data life cycle, reference data and data protection. It works across all statistical products and domains. It makes sure that data can be found, understood, trusted and reused. The data lifecycle management processes (DLM) realise this area.
2.1


FUN-7.1
Govern data
This function sets the rules for data management in the NSI. It defines data policies, standards and responsibilities. It assigns data owners, data stewards and data custodians. It resolves issues that cross domain boundaries. It monitors compliance with the data policies.
2.1.1, 4.1.2


FUN-7.2
Manage metadata
This function captures, maintains and publishes metadata. Metadata describes concepts, variables, classifications, datasets, methods and processes. The function maintains the catalogue in which data can be found. It makes sure that metadata is captured when data is created. It applies international standards, such as GSIM and SDMX.
2.1.2


FUN-7.3
Manage data lifecycle and storage
This function manages data from creation to disposal. It covers quality gates, registration, versioning, storage, retention and disposal. It keeps track of lineage, from output back to source. It makes sure that earlier versions remain available when they are needed. The function applies the design rules of the steady-state model.
2.1.1


FUN-7.4
Manage reference and master data
This function manages the data that other data depends on. Examples are classifications, code lists, statistical registers and population frames. It controls versions and announces changes in advance. It makes sure that all domains use the same version. The function is the single source of truth for reference data.
2.1.4


FUN-7.5
Protect data
This function protects data according to its classification. It applies measures for availability, integrity and confidentiality. It manages pseudonymisation and the keys used for it. It keeps keys separate from the data they protect. The function works closely with information security and privacy management.

FUN-8
Microdata Services
This area gives researchers controlled access to microdata. It covers authorisation, data preparation, secure environments and output control. It also supports analysis without moving data, using privacy-preserving techniques. The NSI remains responsible for confidentiality throughout. FUN-8.1

This function prepares the datasets for each approved project. It selects only the data that the project needs. It applies project-specific pseudonyms, so that data cannot be linked across projects. 2.2.4, 3.3.1

This function provides and runs the environments in which researchers work. It controls who may enter and what may leave. It provides tools and computing power. It logs all activity. It removes data and workspaces when projects end.

FUN-8.4
Control research output
This function checks all results before they leave the secure environment. It applies disclosure control rules to tables, models and other output. It checks for risks across outputs, such as differencing between similar results. It keeps a record of every release. The function protects respondents while allowing research to proceed.
1.3.7

This function makes analysis possible without bringing all data together. It uses techniques such as federated analysis and secure multi-party computation. It defines the trust model, the linkage method and the output rules for each setup. It works with partners who cannot or may not share their data. The function extends microdata services beyond the data the NSI holds itself.

Until then, the services, events and objects of each value stream are described in attribute 8 of the Statistical Data Value Chain chapter, and the objects handed over between value streams in the Steady-State Architecture.

title: Business Architecture
text:
Why the SAF offers more than one model NSIs differ in size, mandate, legal context, data volumes, and technology platform. A single prescribed arrangement would fit some offices well and others poorly. The SAF therefore describes reference models: alternative, internally consistent ways of organising the value chain. Each model answers the same four questions:

At which points is data persisted and made available for reuse?
Which quality criteria must data meet at each point?
Who is accountable for the data at each point?
How are confidentiality and traceability guaranteed along the chain?

The SAF currently describes two reference models. Both follow the same underlying idea, progressive improvement of data through defined layers, but they differ in granularity and in where they place governance.
Model A: Steady-State Architecture
The Steady-State Architecture organises the value chain into business domains that are loosely coupled through five numbered steady states (#1 Raw, #2 Standardized, #3 Processed, #4 Statistics, #5 Released). Each state represents a specific kind of statistical value and has its own quality gate, ownership, and handover interface. The model is derived from production practice in NSIs with many statistical domains and extensive microdata reuse. It is described in full in the remainder of this chapter.
Model B: Medallion Architecture
The Medallion Architecture organises data into three layers of increasing quality, usually called Bronze (raw), Silver (cleansed and conformed), and Gold (curated for consumption). The pattern originates from lakehouse platforms and is a logical design pattern rather than a product. Its strength lays in its simplicity. There are three layers, a clear direction of flow, and the ability to rebuild any layer from the one below it.
As a data-engineering pattern, Medallion does not by itself define statistical semantics, accountability, or confidentiality rules per layer.

The criteria below help an NSI decide which model fits best. They are indicative. No single criterion is decisive, and the SAF toolkit will provide a structured assessment.

Practice within the SAF community indicates that smaller NSIs often adopt a Medallion arrangement, while larger NSIs with many domains tend towards finer-grained states. This observation is to be substantiated through the SAF toolkit assessments.



The models are not mutually exclusive. The steady states can be mapped onto Medallion layers, which allows an NSI to use Medallion as its platform convention while governing data through steady states, or to start with Medallion and introduce finer states as it grows.

title: VS-03 Data Editing and Enrichment
text:
VS-03 is where the quality of the data is actively improved. Standardised data is rarely clean: it contains errors, inconsistencies, gaps, and values that are not yet coded. VS-03 detects these problems, corrects them, fills the gaps, and derives the additional variables that analysis needs. It is the only value stream that deliberately changes values. What makes that safe is full traceability: every change is recorded against its original value, and a reproducible, versioned dataset is produced. The value created is data reliability and analytical readiness. The output is Processed Data: reliable, complete microdata that estimation and modelling can build on.
VS-03 improves the quality of microdata. It does not produce estimates or aggregates: estimation, weighting, aggregation, and statistical modelling belong to VS-04 Estimation, Analysis and Statistical Modeling.
VS-03 corresponds to the business domain Editing, derivation, and non-response correction (see Steady-State Architecture, Business domains). This section describes the business layer of that domain for all four process types: Design, Implementation, Execution, and Management.






NoteSignature discipline: full traceability



Unlike VS-02, which never alters a value, VS-03 deliberately changes values to improve quality. Every edit, imputation, and derivation is rule-based, documented with a reason, attributable (who, which rule, when), and reversible. The original value is preserved beside the processed value, imputed values are flagged, and every version is reproducible. The invariant is no undocumented or irreversible change.








PLACEHOLDER: ArchiMate view VS-03 (a) value stream and capabilities









VS-03 is the third primary value stream. It receives Standardized Data from VS-02 and turns it into trustworthy, analytically sound input for estimation and modelling.
VS-03 takes data from State #2 to State #3. Before VS-03, the data is structurally aligned and coded to standards, with its values unchanged. After VS-03, its content has been validated, corrected, completed, and enriched, integrated with other datasets where applicable, with new derived variables and fully documented lineage. The quality gate, the minimum metadata set, and the protection of State #3 are described in State #3: Processed Data and are not repeated here. Where a product skips State #2, VS-03 consumes State #1 directly.
VS-02 deliberately leaves all value-changing work to VS-03. Together with the standardised data, VS-03 receives the metadata VS-02 attached: the recorded unit, currency, and reference-period bases, the records of definition differences, and the list of unmapped or uncoded values. VS-03 then performs the operations VS-02 deferred: interpretive coding of free text and value reconciliation across sources (VS-03.2), and unit and currency conversion, reference-period alignment, and derivation (VS-03.4).

The stage starts when the Standardized Data Registered event is received from VS-02. The designed detection rules run on the incoming dataset: consistency, range, outlier, duplicate, and completeness checks. Selective-editing scores are computed, so that effort goes to the problems that matter for the results. The outcome is a diagnostic report that gives the location and type of each suspected error, its severity, and its disposition: auto-correct, flag for review, or accept. No values are changed yet. The following principles govern VS-03 most directly.








Principle
Statement
Application in VS-03




SAF-P01
Actively participate in open-source communities to maintain collective control over statistical processes
Editing, imputation, and coding tooling, such as selective-editing engines and imputation libraries, is developed and shared in open-source communities with other NSIs. This keeps collective control over critical methodological capabilities instead of depending on vendors.


SAF-P07
Implement loosely coupled processes and systems
Editing is independent from upstream standardisation and downstream estimation. Processed Data (State #3) is the decoupling interface: downstream consumers use edited, enriched microdata without knowing how it was corrected or imputed.


SAF-P08
Data is shared property
Processed data, once versioned, is available to all authorised consumers. Editing and enrichment are not duplicated across statistical products when the same processed asset can serve several purposes.


SAF-P09
No data without metadata and classification
Every edit, imputation, and derived variable carries metadata: the rule applied, the original value, the imputation method and flag, the derivation formula, and a classification for derived variables. This makes the changes transparent and reproducible.


SAF-P10
Security by design
Access controls, integrity verification, and a tamper-evident edit audit trail are built into the editing pipeline from the start, so that every change to a value stays attributable and traceable.


SAF-P11
Privacy by design
VS-03 works on pseudonymised microdata. Enrichment and integration with other datasets raise the risk of re-identification, so linkage is assessed for disclosure risk and minimisation by design, not afterwards.









NotePrinciples that apply across the process types



SAF-P09 is the backbone of the editing discipline: Design defines the rules and the required edit metadata, Execution captures the original value, rule, and reason for every change, and Management assesses edit quality and closes gaps. SAF-P10 governs the tamper-evident edit audit trail across all stages, VS-03.1 to VS-03.5. SAF-P11 applies especially to Design Integration and Linkage Rules and to VS-03.4, where linkage can raise the risk of re-identification. SAF-P07 governs both the intake of State #2 from VS-02 and the handover of State #3 to VS-04.

Structural Business Statistics. The design sets consistency rules (turnover ≥ 0, employees ≥ 0, turnover per employee within a plausible band by NACE class), outlier rules based on a Hidiroglou–Berthelot test on year-on-year ratios, and a selective-editing score that flags only units whose potential error would move a published aggregate by more than a set threshold. Everything else is accepted without manual work. In a cycle, the standardised SBS file is diagnosed: 312 units fail the turnover-per-employee band, 47 are duplicates, and 1,204 have missing employee counts. The selective-editing scores prioritise 89 units whose potential error would materially affect a published aggregate; the remaining low-impact flags are scheduled for automatic treatment.
Labour Force Survey imputation. For item non-response on income, about 9% of records, the design specifies regression imputation with age, education (ISCED), occupation (ISCO), and region as predictors, and a constraint that imputed income stays within the valid range of the respondent’s earnings bracket. Each imputed income carries the flag imputed=true and the method code REG-01, and the predictor values used are recorded. Analysts can exclude or down-weight imputed values, and the imputation can be reproduced or revised.
Labour Force Survey coding. The 42,000 free-text occupation answers handed over from VS-02 are coded to ISCO-08. 88% are coded automatically at or above the confidence threshold of 0.85, 5,040 go to computer-assisted coding, and 1,200 ambiguous cases go to expert manual coding. Each coded value records the source text, the assigned code, the method, and the confidence, so it is auditable as an editing decision.
Price statistics. The implementation team builds an outlier detector for daily price changes, an editing engine that applies designed corrections such as decimal-point fixes, and a review queue for flagged price jumps. Every correction stores the original scraped price, the rule, and the analyst’s adjudication, so the edit can be audited and reversed.
Tax register to business statistics. Turnover, recorded by VS-02 in thousands of euro on a fiscal-year basis, is converted to units on a calendar-year basis with the designed conversion and apportionment rules. The conversion factor and the original value are stored in the lineage. Turnover per employee is then derived as a new indicator, with its formula and inputs recorded.

title: VS-03 Data Editing and Enrichment
text:
VS-03 is where the quality of the data is actively improved. Standardised data is rarely clean: it contains errors, inconsistencies, gaps, and values that are not yet coded. VS-03 detects these problems, corrects them, fills the gaps, and derives the additional variables that analysis needs. It is the only value stream that deliberately changes values. What makes that safe is full traceability: every change is recorded against its original value, and a reproducible, versioned dataset is produced. The value created is data reliability and analytical readiness. The output is Processed Data: reliable, complete microdata that estimation and modelling can build on.
VS-03 improves the quality of microdata. It does not produce estimates or aggregates: estimation, weighting, aggregation, and statistical modelling belong to VS-04 Estimation, Analysis and Statistical Modeling.
VS-03 corresponds to the business domain Editing, derivation, and non-response correction (see Steady-State Architecture, Business domains). This section describes the business layer of that domain for all four process types: Design, Implementation, Execution, and Management.






NoteSignature discipline: full traceability



Unlike VS-02, which never alters a value, VS-03 deliberately changes values to improve quality. Every edit, imputation, and derivation is rule-based, documented with a reason, attributable (who, which rule, when), and reversible. The original value is preserved beside the processed value, imputed values are flagged, and every version is reproducible. The invariant is no undocumented or irreversible change.








PLACEHOLDER: ArchiMate view VS-03 (a) value stream and capabilities









VS-03 is the third primary value stream. It receives Standardized Data from VS-02 and turns it into trustworthy, analytically sound input for estimation and modelling.
VS-03 takes data from State #2 to State #3. Before VS-03, the data is structurally aligned and coded to standards, with its values unchanged. After VS-03, its content has been validated, corrected, completed, and enriched, integrated with other datasets where applicable, with new derived variables and fully documented lineage. The quality gate, the minimum metadata set, and the protection of State #3 are described in State #3: Processed Data and are not repeated here. Where a product skips State #2, VS-03 consumes State #1 directly.
VS-02 deliberately leaves all value-changing work to VS-03. Together with the standardised data, VS-03 receives the metadata VS-02 attached: the recorded unit, currency, and reference-period bases, the records of definition differences, and the list of unmapped or uncoded values. VS-03 then performs the operations VS-02 deferred: interpretive coding of free text and value reconciliation across sources (VS-03.2), and unit and currency conversion, reference-period alignment, and derivation (VS-03.4).

The stages describe the value that VS-03 adds in every production cycle. Together they form the execution process type of VS-03. In a mature steady state, the rules and methods have been designed and built in advance (see attribute 4). Execution then focuses on running the cycle, applying edits, imputations, and derivations, and capturing the full edit lineage so that every value change is documented and reversible.

Value created: A clear, prioritised picture of where the data is wrong, incomplete, or inconsistent.
The stage starts when the Standardized Data Registered event is received from VS-02. The designed detection rules run on the incoming dataset: consistency, range, outlier, duplicate, and completeness checks. Selective-editing scores are computed, so that effort goes to the problems that matter for the results. The outcome is a diagnostic report that gives the location and type of each suspected error, its severity, and its disposition: auto-correct, flag for review, or accept. No values are changed yet. This stage diagnoses; correction happens in VS-03.2.

Value created: Errors corrected and inconsistencies resolved, with every change documented and reversible.
Auto-correction rules are applied to the records that the design earmarked for automatic treatment. Flagged records go to subject-matter statisticians, who adjudicate and correct them. For every change, the editing engine records the original value, the rule or decision applied, a reason code, the actor, and a timestamp. The edit is therefore fully attributable and reversible. This stage also carries out the interpretive coding handed over from VS-02, for example coding free-text occupation to ISCO, the international occupation classification, with low-confidence cases reviewed. Where integrated sources disagree on a value, the designed value-reconciliation rules are applied. No edit may leave a record that violates the validation rules.

Value created: Complete datasets where gaps are filled with the best available estimate, clearly flagged as imputed.
Missing and non-response values are filled with the designed imputation methods. The method is chosen per variable and missingness pattern: deterministic, donor (hot-deck or nearest-neighbor), model-based, or external-source. Acceptance constraints make sure that imputed values still satisfy the edit rules. Every imputed value receives an imputation flag and a method code, so that imputed and observed values are always distinguishable downstream, and the imputation inputs are recorded in the lineage. Imputed values never overwrite observed values; they fill only genuine gaps.
